sections.text: Antibacterial and Antifungal Potential of Hermetia illucens Hemolymph Contained-Peptides

Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) constitute a chemically and structurally heterogeneous family of molecules produced by a wide range of living organisms, including plants, fish, amphibians, mammals, and insects. Their expression is particularly high in hosts frequently exposed to microorganisms, where AMPs play a key role in innate immune responses. Insects represent one of the richest natural sources of AMPs. Over their long evolutionary history, they have developed a highly efficient immune system with AMPs playing a central role in defense against pathogens, enabling them to colonize various habitats. In recent years, interest in AMPs has significantly increased due to the emergence of antibiotic resistance, positioning these peptides as potential therapeutic alternatives for treating infections caused by multi-resistant pathogens. In this study, we investigated the antimicrobial activity of peptide fractions extracted from the hemolymph of Hermetia illucens larvae (Diptera, Stratiomyidae), an insect known for its high expression of AMPs. Larvae were injected separately with either Escherichia coli (Gram-negative) or Micrococcus flavus (Gram-positive), and hemolymph was collected 24 h post-infection, as well as from uninfected larvae. Antimicrobial activity was assessed through microbiological assays, including both agar diffusion tests and microdilution assays. Results demonstrated significant activity against pathogenic bacterial strains, including antibiotic-resistant ones. The Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC) and Minimum Bactericidal Concentration (MBC) were determined for each experimental condition. MIC values ranged from 0.023 to 0.375 µg·µL⁻ 1 , while MBC values ranged from 0.187 to 0.750 µg·µL⁻ 1 , depending on the bacterial strain and the infection treatment group. These findings demonstrate the potential of H. illucens -derived AMPs as effective agents against Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, including resistant strains, and support their further development as alternatives or adjuvants to conventional antibiotics. Introduction Antibiotics have represented one of the most significant revolutions in the history of medicine, drastically reducing mortality from bacterial infections. The term “antibiotic” was introduced by Waksman in 1947 to describe chemical compounds produced by microorganisms capable of inhibiting the growth of other microorganisms [ 1 ]. However, the use of antimicrobial substances dates back to much earlier times, as ancient civilizations like the Egyptians and Greeks already used moldy bread and plant-based substances to treat infections [ 2 , 3 ]. The beginning of the modern antibiotic era was marked by the discovery of mycophenolic acid in 1893, followed by the discovery of penicillin by Alexander Fleming in 1928, which revolutionized the treatment of infectious diseases [ 4 – 6 ]. Despite the success of antibiotics, antimicrobial resistance (AMR) quickly emerged as one of the most critical challenges to global health. Resistance to the first antibiotics, notably penicillin, was documented as early as the 1940 s, with the emergence of resistant strains of Staphylococcus aureus [ 7 ]. Other antibiotics, including methicillin (introduced in 1959), faced resistance within a year of their introduction [ 8 ]. This phenomenon extended to new classes of antibiotics, such as vancomycin, contributing to today’s alarming increase in multidrug-resistant bacteria [ 9 ]. Italy, in particular, registers high rates of antibiotic resistance and the highest number of related deaths in Europe, with approximately 11,000 of the 33,000 deaths annually caused by antibiotic-resistant infections [ 10 ]. By 2050, it is estimated that AMR could cause up to 10 million deaths per year, with associated costs exceeding 100 trillion euros [ 11 ]. Antimicrobial resistance develops through various mechanisms. Bacteria can inactivate or modify antibiotics through specific enzymes, alter the molecular targets of the antibiotic, reduce membrane permeability, or increase drug efflux through efflux pumps [ 12 ]. These adaptive mechanisms make treating bacterial infections increasingly difficult, reducing the effectiveness of available drugs. Acquired resistance, through the horizontal transfer of genes between bacteria (e.g., by conjugation or transduction), further contributes to the rapid spread of resistant strains, such as those producing carbapenemases [ 13 ]. One of the most promising solutions to this growing crisis is represented by antimicrobial peptides (AMPs), a class of small bioactive proteins naturally produced by living organisms. These peptides are part of the innate immune response and possess a broad range of activity against bacteria, fungi, and viruses. Their amphipathic structure, with both hydrophobic and hydrophilic regions, allows them to interact with bacterial membranes, leading to cell lysis [ 14 , 15 ]. AMPs offer several advantages over traditional antibiotics, including a lower tendency to induce resistance and side effects, as well as broad-spectrum activity [ 16 ]. AMPs can be categorized based on their origin. They have been isolated from a wide range of sources, including mammals, amphibians, microorganisms, and plants [ 17 ]. However, recent attention has focused on insects, which are known to produce significant amounts of AMPs to survive in microbe-rich environments [ 18 , 19 ]. Among insects, Hermetia illucens , known as the black soldier fly, has garnered considerable interest for its ability to bioconvert organic waste and for producing a wide range of AMPs [ 20 ]. The larvae of H. illucens , which feed on decomposing organic substrates, have been studied for their ability to express more than 50 AMP-encoding genes [ 21 ]. Studies have shown that stimulating the larvae’s immune system can enhance the production of peptides active against resistant pathogens such as S. aureus and Escherichia coli [ 22 – 24 ]. Besides AMPs, H. illucens larvae contain antimicrobial lipids that have significant antimicrobial activity against MDR Aeromonas spp ., hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae , and phytopathogenic bacterial strains [ 25 – 28 ]. The life cycle of H. illucens consists of five distinct stages: egg, larva, prepupa, pupa, and adult, with the larval stage being the longest and most active [ 29 , 30 ]. During this stage, the larvae accumulate resources and produce AMPs to defend themselves against environmental threats. Several peptides isolated from H. illucens , including defensins, cecropins, and attacins, have shown potent antibacterial activity against both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, as well as antifungal properties [ 31 , 32 ]. Several recent studies stated the emergence of multidrug-resistant bacterial pathogens from different origins, which enhances the necessity for new active and safe alternatives for antibiotics. Besides, the routine application of antimicrobial sensitivity testing detects the antibiotic of choice as well as the isolation of emerging MDR [ 33 – 36 ]. Within this context, the exploration of AMPs derived from H. illucens represents a valuable opportunity to expand the portfolio of naturally occurring antimicrobials with potential biomedical relevance. Although several AMPs have been identified in H. illucens , their full spectrum of bioactivity and therapeutic potential is still not comprehensively investigated. The aim of this study is to explore bioactive compounds of entomological origin derived from H. illucens for the development of AMPs as a new class of safe and effective molecules. The study aims to enrich current knowledge and contribute to the identification of promising agents against drug-resistant pathogens. The findings may provide a basis for innovative therapeutic approaches, with potential implications for future antimicrobial development in clinical and preventive contexts.

Materials and Methods Hermetia illucens Rearing Hermetia illucens larvae were provided by Xflies s.r.l (Potenza, Italy). After egg hatching, larvae were fed on a standard Gainesville diet (30% alfalfa, 50% wheat bran, 20% corn meal) [ 37 ] at 70% moisture under controlled conditions of temperature (27 ± 1.0 °C), relative humidity (70% ± 5%) and photoperiod (12L:12D (h)) [ 38 ]. H. illucens Larval Infection and Hemolymph Collection Escherichia coli (Gram-negative, LMG:2092 strain) and Micrococcus flavus (Gram-positive, DSM 19079) were incubated in 10 mL of Luria Bertani (LB) broth at 37 °C for 24 h, under shaking. A total of 1 mL of each bacterial culture was inoculated into a fresh LB broth, incubated at 37 °C and used for the experiment once the optical density (OD) at 600 nm reached 1. Fifth instar larvae of H. illucens were firstly washed with 70% ethanol and sterile water and then infected via a capillary dipped into the cell suspension of E. coli or M. flavus [ 39 , 40 ] in order to stimulate the production of different AMPs and/or to induce a higher expression level of constitutively expressed AMPs. Following the bacterial challenge, larvae were left in a controlled chamber at 27 °C for 24 h. A group of uninfected larvae was used as control. For each treatment, 100 larvae were used. To facilitate the collection of hemolymph, sterile capillaries were used to puncture the abdomens of larvae. Hemolymph from both infected and uninfected larvae was collected, using a pipette (Gilson, Middleton, WI, USA), in ice-cold tubes, containing a fixed-minimum quantity of L-ascorbic acid (0.015 g) (Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany), to prevent hemolymph melanization. To isolate the plasma (cell-free hemolymph) and remove the cellular components, the extracted hemolymph was subjected to centrifugation at 10,000 rpm for 5 min at 4 °C. The recovered supernatant (plasma) was stored at − 80 °C until use (Fig. 1 ). Fig. 1 Workflow of AMP extraction from H. illucens larvae: from bacterial injection to peptide purification. The process includes larval injection, hemolymph collection, protein precipitation, final PF recovery and in vitro tests Isolation of Peptide Fraction via Organic Solvent Precipitation In order to separate the putative AMPs in the hemolymph from the higher molecular weight proteins, the plasma recovered from both uninfected and infected larvae was subjected to a precipitation protocol with methanol (Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany), acetic acid (Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany) and water in a 90:1:9 v/v ratio. This method promotes the selective precipitation of high-molecular-weight proteins while maintaining low-molecular-weight peptides in solution. The plasma and solvent were mixed in a 1:9 v/v ratio and then centrifuged for 45 min at 13,000 rpm at 4 °C (Fig. 1 ). To remove possible traces of lipids that could be co-extracted due to the use of methanol, a further treatment with hexane was performed [ 41 ]. The obtained supernatant, containing the Peptide Fraction (PF), compounds with a molecular weight lower than 30 kDa [ 42 ], was then vacuum-dried to remove the organic solvents and resuspended in a volume of sterile water equal to the original plasma volume. The molecular weight distribution and identity of the peptides extracted through this protocol were previously characterized via SDS-PAGE and mass spectrometry, as reported in Scieuzo et al. (2023), whereas the peptide sequences are available in the Supplementary Materials of the same publication, since the present study represents a continuation of that work [ 41 ]. All samples were subsequently stored at 4 °C until the next use. Protein Quantification via Bradford Assay The protein concentrations of all samples were quantified with Bio-Rad Protein Assay, Dye Reagent Concentrate (Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA, USA), according to the Bradford method [ 43 ]. To calculate the concentration of the proteins, a standard calibration using known concentrations of the Bovine Serum Albumin (BSA) protein (Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany) was set up. The absorbance of the samples was measured at a wavelength of 595 nm using a spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). Bacterial Strains and Culture Conditions E. coli (LMG:2092), M. flavus (DSM 19079) were cultured on Luria–Bertani Broth (LB) and agar (Oxoid Ltd); Pseudomonas aeruginosa (ATCC® 9027™) and Proteus mirabilis were cultured on Brain Heart Infusion (BHI) broth and agar (Oxoid Ltd); Staphylococcus aureus (ATCC® 6538™), Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica serovar Typhimurium (ATCC® 14028GFP™), Enteroinvasive Escherichia coli (EIEC) (ATCC® 43,893™), Enterococcus faecalis (ATCC® 9027™), Streptococcus pyogenes , carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae , and methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus were cultured on Tryptic Soy Broth (TSB) and Tryptic Soy Agar (TSA) (Oxoid Ltd); Candida albicans (ATCC® 10,231™) was cultured on Sabouraud Dextrose Broth (SDB) and Sabouraud Dextrose Agar (SDA) (Oxoid Ltd). Evaluation of the Antibacterial Activity of PF via Agar Diffusion Assay The agar diffusion assay was used to evaluate the antimicrobial activity of the PF in vitro. A single colony of each bacterial strain was transferred to the appropriate culture medium and incubated overnight at 37 °C with constant agitation. Subsequently, 100 μL of bacterial suspension, adjusted to an optical density of 0.3 at 600 nm (OD600), was uniformly spread onto solid medium plates using a sterile cotton swab. Following absorption of the bacterial suspension into the medium, holes were drilled on the plates and 100 μL of PF derived from the hemolymph of both infected and uninfected larvae were added in duplicate. Sterile water was used as a negative control. Plates were incubated overnight at 37 °C [ 44 ]. Evaluation of the Minimum Inhibitory Concentration of the PF via Microdilution Assay Microdilution assays were conducted on PF to determine the Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC), the lowest concentration of an antimicrobial agent capable of inhibiting the growth of a microorganism in vitro after 12–24 h of incubation. This value is obtained by testing a standard concentration of microorganisms against a series of scalar dilutions of the antimicrobial substance [ 45 ]. Specifically, the microdilution assay was performed by serial dilutions in 96-well microplates, adding scalar doses of the antimicrobial agent, followed by inoculation with the bacterial strain at a constant concentration. After incubation, bacterial growth was assessed based on turbidity. For the assay, eight serial dilutions were prepared (0.750 µg·µL⁻ 1 , 0.375 µg·µL⁻ 1 , 0.187 µg·µL⁻ 1 , 0.093 µg·µL⁻ 1 , 0.046 µg·µL⁻ 1 , 0.023 µg·µL⁻ 1 , 0.011 µg·µL⁻ 1 , 0.0058 µg·µL⁻ 1 ). The bacterial strains tested against the PF were diluted to an optical density at 600 nm of 0.3. In each well of the microplate, 100 µL of medium and 100 µL of the antimicrobial agent were added to the first row, with an initial concentration of 0.750 µg·µL⁻ 1 . Serial dilutions were then performed directly in the plate, and 1 µL of bacterial culture at OD 0.3 was added to each well. The controls used included a negative control with only the medium, a positive control with the medium and 1 µL of bacterial culture at OD 0.3, and a substance control with 100 µL of medium and 100 µL of the antimicrobial agent being tested. Evaluation of Minimum Bactericidal Assay of the PF The Minimum Bactericidal Concentration (MBC) was determined as the lowest concentration of PF required to kill 99.9% of the initial microbial population after 24 h [ 46 ]. Specifically, the microdilution assay was performed by serial dilutions in 96-well microplates, adding scalar doses of the antimicrobial agent, followed by inoculation with the bacterial strain at a constant concentration. Serial dilutions were then performed directly in the plate, and 1 µL of bacterial culture at OD 0.3 was added to each well. Discussion In this study, we focused on the in vitro evaluation of the antimicrobial activity of PFs extracted from the hemolymph of H. illucens following infection with the Gram-negative bacterium E. coli or the Gram-positive bacterium M. flavus . Microbiological assays were carried out against a selection of human pathogenic strains, including multi-resistant strains such as carbapenem-resistant K. pneumoniae and methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA). These strains pose a significant public health threat due to their resistance to traditional antibiotic treatments. Among tested bacteria, enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC), a Gram-negative bacterium known for its ability to penetrate the colonic mucosa, multiply within epithelial cells, and spread, causing inflammation and damage to the intestinal barrier, resulting in clinical manifestations of dysentery, was analyzed [ 47 ]. The results showed that the PFs obtained from larvae infected with E. coli exhibited greater antimicrobial efficacy against EIEC, as evidenced by the Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC) value of 0.023 µg·µL⁻ 1 , which was lower than that of the control samples and those obtained from larvae infected with M. flavus . Similarly, the minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC) values confirmed this trend, with 0.375 µg·µL⁻ 1 recorded for control fraction, while a value of 0.750 µg·µL⁻ 1 was observed for both the fractions derived from larvae infected with E. coli and M. flavus . Further tests on P. aeruginosa demonstrated that the PF obtained from uninfected larvae exhibited greater antimicrobial activity compared to those derived from larvae infected with E. coli and M. flavus , with a MIC of 0.093 µg·µL⁻ 1 for the control sample. Bactericidal activity was detected at 0.375 µg·µL⁻ 1 for the fractions obtained from control larvae and those infected with E. coli , whereas a higher concentration (0.750 µg·µL⁻ 1 ) was required for the fractions derived from larvae infected with M. flavus . P. aeruginosa , part of the ESKAPE group, is a Gram-negative bacterium known for its antibiotic resistance, and the WHO classifies it as a critical priority pathogen due to its ability to cause severe respiratory and systemic infections, particularly in immunocompromised patients [ 48 ]. Similarly, tests on S. aureus revealed consistent antimicrobial activity across all samples, regardless of bacterial stimulation, suggesting the intrinsic antimicrobial potential of the PFs. S. aureus is a Gram-positive bacterium responsible not only for skin infections, such as boils and abscesses, but also for more severe conditions like pneumonia, endocarditis, and sepsis [ 49 ]. For S. aureus , uniform MIC and MBC values of 0.093 µg·µL⁻ 1 and 0.750 µg·µL⁻ 1 , respectively, were observed for all tested fractions. Against S. Typhimurium, a Gram-negative bacterium known for causing gastrointestinal infections [ 50 ], no significant differences were observed between the control and stimulated fractions with MIC values of 0.093 µg·µL⁻ 1 and MBC values of 0.187 µg·µL⁻ 1 . Tests on S. pyogenes , a Gram-positive bacterium that causes infections such as pharyngitis and skin diseases [ 51 ], demonstrated strong antimicrobial activity, with lower MIC values: 0.046 µg·µL⁻ 1 for fractions derived from uninfected larvae and infected with M. flavus and 0.023 µg·µL⁻ 1 for those from larvae infected with E. coli . However, only the highest concentration showed bactericidal activity (0.750 µg·µL⁻ 1 for control and M. flavus -infected larvae), while no bactericidal activity was observed for the fractions from larvae infected with E. coli . Further tests were conducted on E. faecalis , a Gram-positive bacterium that is a commensal of the gastrointestinal tract and responsible for urinary tract infections and other nosocomial infections, especially in immunocompromised individuals [ 52 ]. Antimicrobial activity tests revealed MIC values of 0.093 µg·µL⁻ 1 across all tested conditions and MBC values of 0.375 µg·µL⁻ 1 . Subsequent tests were conducted on P. mirabilis , a Gram-negative bacterium known to be one of the main causative agents of urinary tract infections. A single bacterial strain can respond differently to antimicrobial treatment due to phenotypic variability within the bacterial population. This phenotypic heterogeneity may arise from differing responses to slightly divergent tissue microenvironments or from genetic circuits where small endogenous fluctuations in a limited number of transcription factors drive gene expression, combined with a positive feedback loop [ 57 ]. Additionally, bacterial persistence is an example of phenotypic variation, where genetically identical bacterial populations respond heterogeneously to antibiotic treatment. This phenomenon allows a small proportion of cells to survive the treatment even at very high drug concentrations [ 58 , 59 ]. Persistence is not related to genetic resistance but rather to phenotypic variations that may be influenced by memory of past environments [ 58 ]. Finally, bacteria can acquire resistance through de novo mutations or by acquiring resistance genes from other organisms. These mechanisms may enable the production of enzymes that degrade the drug, the expression of efflux systems that prevent the drug from reaching its intracellular target, the modification of the drug’s target site, or the production of an alternative metabolic pathway [ 60 ].

The antimicrobial activity results against MRSA show a MIC value of 0.375 µg·µL⁻ 1 , consistent across both the PFs from control larvae and those from larvae infected with E. coli and M. flavus . This suggests that stimulation with Gram-positive strains may enhance the antimicrobial response against bacteria of the same group.

The PFs obtained through organic solvent precipitation were tested for their potential antifungal activity against C. albicans . C. albicans is a common commensal fungus that can become an opportunistic pathogen, causing infections ranging from superficial to life-threatening systemic candidiasis [ 61 ]. It can affect various body sites, including the oral cavity, gastrointestinal tract, and vaginal tract [ 62 ]. The fungus can enter the bloodstream through epithelial damage or medical devices, leading to potential organ infections, particularly in immunocompromised individuals, who are at higher risk for invasive infections with high mortality rates [ 63 ].

The results indicate strong antifungal activity against C. albicans . The MIC assay shows a minimum inhibitory concentration of 0.375 µg·µL⁻ 1 for the PFs from control larvae and larvae infected with E. coli , and 0.187 µg·µL⁻ 1 for the fraction from larvae infected with M. flavus . The MBC values are 0.750 µg·µL⁻ 1 for the fractions from control larvae and those infected with E. coli , and 0.375 µg·µL⁻ 1 for the fraction from larvae infected with M. flavus . These findings suggest that stimulation with Gram-positive bacteria enhances the response against C. albicans . AMPs from insects, particularly H. illucens , show promise as alternatives to conventional antibiotics and antifungal against various pathogens, including C. albicans . Studies have identified numerous AMPs in H. illucens with potential antibacterial and antifungal activities [ 22 ]. These peptides can disrupt cell membranes, inhibit filamentation, and combat biofilms of C. albicans [ 64 , 65 ]. Synthetic peptides designed to mimic natural AMPs have also demonstrated potent anticandidal effects with low hemolytic activity [ 66 , 67 ]. The efficacy of AMPs against C. albicans depends on factors such as amphipathicity, cationicity, and helical structure [ 68 ]. Combining AMPs with conventional antifungals may enhance their therapeutic potential [ 66 , 69 ]. Bacterial cell membranes possess unique components—such as abundant peptidoglycan and distinct lipid profiles—that allow cationic AMPs to bind with high specificity. This high affinity is due to the peptide interaction with the negatively charged surface and other unique features of bacterial membranes, which are not present in the lipid-rich membranes of human cells. As a result, AMPs generally do not exert cytotoxic effects on healthy mammalian cells: their interactions with human cell membranes are much weaker than with Gram-positive or Gram-negative bacterial membranes [ 41 ]. Similarly, fungal cell membranes differ from those of human cells by containing ergosterol instead of cholesterol and having a higher proportion of negatively charged lipids, which facilitates selective AMP binding and membrane disruption.

This pathogen-specific targeting is supported by evidence that AMPs can modulate host immune responses and reduce inflammatory damage, thereby promoting a healthy cellular environment. Indeed, many studies have shown that insect-derived AMPs – including those identified in H. illucens – exhibit broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity with minimal toxicity toward eukaryotic cells [ 40 ]. For example, Elhag et al. ( 40 ) reported that H. illucens AMPs display wide-ranging antibacterial potency while remaining harmless to mammalian cells [ 40 ]. Likewise, peptides derived from mammalian lectins (e.g., CLEC3A) have been shown to have no direct cytotoxicity against healthy human cells even at microbicidal concentrations.

Importantly, AMPs generally show relatively low off-target toxicity to mammalian cells, further highlighting their promise as safe alternatives to conventional antibiotics. Fritsche et al. ( 70 ) have emphasized that AMPs typically exhibit “relatively low collateral toxic effects on mammalian cells,” underscoring their potential for therapeutic use without harming host tissues. Together, these observations underscore the selective mechanism of action of insect AMPs and support their use as effective yet host-compatible antimicrobial agents [ 70 ].

Conclusions This study highlights the potential of AMPs derived from H. illucens hemolymph as promising antimicrobial candidates against a broad spectrum of pathogenic strains, including multi-resistant bacteria. The results indicate that H. illucens AMPs exhibit activity against both Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, with a specific response to infections induced by E. coli and M. flavus . The observed in vitro efficacy against multi-resistant pathogens, such as carbapenem-resistant K. pneumoniae (CRKP) and methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA), highlights the relevance of these peptides for further investigations. Moreover, the ability of H. illucens immune response to modulate AMPs production according to the type of infection suggests the possibility to identify novel antimicrobial molecules with selective activity. Future studies will be addressed to the identification and characterization of the specific AMPs responsible for the observed antimicrobial activity; in addition, structural characterization and stability profiling of the PFs, including its susceptibility to proteolytic degradation and pH sensitivity, will also be explored in future studies to support its therapeutic applicability along with a deeper understanding of the phenotypic dynamics influencing their efficacy against multi-resistant pathogens. The present study provides a foundation for further investigations aimed at harnessing H. illucens AMPs as a viable and sustainable alternative to conventional antibiotics, while emphasizing that additional preclinical research is required to fully assess their therapeutic potential and guide future translational efforts.
